nameStory: Atlantic camas gets its name from its eastern North American range, distinguishing it from western camas species that were crucial food sources for Native American tribes. The word 'camas' comes from the Chinook word 'chamas,' meaning 'sweet,' referring to the edible bulbs that were traditionally harvested and cooked. It's also called wild hyacinth because its tall spikes of blue flowers resemble garden hyacinths.
description: Atlantic camas is a graceful perennial wildflower that grows from a deep bulb, reaching 1-4 feet tall. In late spring, it sends up a striking spike of star-shaped, pale blue to purple flowers that bloom from bottom to top. The plant has long, narrow leaves that emerge from the base in a clump, similar to daffodil foliage. After blooming, it produces small capsules filled with black seeds before the plant goes dormant for the summer.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tall spikes of 6-petaled star-shaped flowers in pale blue to purple, blooming from bottom of spike upward; each flower about 1 inch across with prominent yellow stamens

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves emerge in a basal clump; leaves feel smooth and slightly waxy, with parallel veins running lengthwise

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single tall flower spike rises from center of leaf clump; plant appears similar to a large daffodil before blooming

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Three-chambered capsules split open to reveal shiny black seeds; capsules feel papery when dry and rattle when shaken

habitat: Atlantic camas thrives in moist to wet prairies, meadows, and open woodlands with rich, organic soils. In New England, look for it in low-lying areas that stay moist through spring, such as wet meadows, marshy edges, and prairie remnants. It's extremely rare in our region, with only a few known populations.

seasonality.spring: Narrow leaves emerge early, followed by spectacular flower spikes in May and June that attract native bees and butterflies.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, seed capsules develop and ripen while leaves begin to yellow and die back by midsummer.
seasonality.fall: Plant is completely dormant with only dried seed stalks remaining; seeds disperse from split capsules.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts visible; bulb rests deep underground until next spring's emergence.

funFact: Atlantic camas is incredibly rare in New England with only 3 recorded observations, making it one of our most elusive native wildflowers - you're more likely to spot a moose than find this botanical treasure!
confusionNotes: Wild hyacinth might be confused with cultivated grape hyacinth, but Atlantic camas has much larger, star-shaped flowers in loose spikes rather than tiny bell-shaped flowers in dense clusters. Remember: wild camas has 6-pointed stars, grape hyacinth has tiny bells.
contextualKnowledge: While western camas species were important traditional foods, Atlantic camas should never be harvested due to its extreme rarity in New England and the difficulty of distinguishing edible camas from toxic death camas species. Always admire but never disturb this precious wildflower.
compareHints: Atlantic camas is the only Camassia species native to eastern North America, while great camas is a western species sometimes grown in gardens. Atlantic camas is smaller overall with paler flowers, while great camas has deeper blue-purple flowers and can grow much taller. In New England, any wild camas you find will be the Atlantic species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Great camas is much larger and more robust than its eastern relative Atlantic camas, with taller flower spikes and broader leaves.
